title: My First Week in MDS
text:
My first week in MDS was quite interesting.
I had been preparing for this move for months. Then, quite suddenly, I was sitting on a plane at 3 in the morning wondering how exactly I had agreed to do this.

title: My First Week in MDS
text:
The Flight





I started my flight from India at 3 in the morning.
Twenty hours of travelling, a 4-hour layover in Frankfurt, and several attempts at sleeping later, I landed in Vancouver.
It was 3 in the afternoon.
Apparently, when you cross enough time zones, your birthday starts behaving like a distributed system.






Note



Longest birthday ever: Landing day happened to be my birthday. Crossing that many time zones gave me the longest birthday of my life.
At this point, I had been awake for approximately 47 years, although the exact number is still pending validation.


The slightly strange part was that despite leaving India at 3 AM and travelling for most of the day, Vancouver greeted me with another 3 PM.
My body, meanwhile, had stopped participating in the experiment.

title: My First Week in MDS
text:
Jericho Beach
I stayed in a hostel near Jericho Beach for the first week.
This turned out to be an excellent decision.
I’m a big fan of beaches, so about ten minutes after checking in, I headed out to see it for myself.
I ended up standing there for a while, watching the waves wash over my feet with the evening sun coming down.





After spending roughly a day travelling halfway across the world, it was probably the first moment when it actually felt like:
Okay. I’m here.
And then I remembered I had to figure out where I was going to buy groceries.

title: My First Week in MDS
text:
Orientation
The next day, I attended the MDS Orientation.
After travelling from India, waking up in a new country, and spending the previous day contemplating the meaning of time, suddenly being surrounded by a room full of people who were all about to spend the next year doing the same program was a little surreal.
I met a lot of new people, and one of the things I enjoyed most was hearing everyone’s stories — where they came from, what they had been doing before MDS, and what brought them here.
There was a surprisingly large amount of interesting life experience packed into one cohort.
I’m looking forward to getting to know everyone better over the next year.






Tip



Data Science lesson #1: Meeting an entire cohort at once produces a rather impressive amount of unstructured data.

title: My First Week in MDS
text:
So far
One week in, and the experiment has started.
I’ve moved to a new country, started a new degree, met a lot of new people, found a beach within ten minutes of my hostel, and somehow managed to have a birthday that lasted significantly longer than intended.
Not a bad first week.
Now I just have to survive the rest of the program.
And Vancouver winter.
Those are two separate problems.

title: A Perfect Day in Vancouver
text:
I’d only been in Vancouver for a couple of weeks, so I decided to conduct a fairly ambitious experiment: how much of the city could I see in a single day?
The answer turned out to be quite a lot — although my feet had a different opinion by the end.
I somehow managed to fit a forest, an ocean, a skyline, and a pint of beer into one day, all before sunset.

title: A Perfect Day in Vancouver
text:
Stanley Park
First stop: Stanley Park.
I’d heard it was big, but walking into it still caught me off guard — massive trees on one side, the ocean on the other, and a seawall that just keeps going.
I spent the morning wandering the trails, half expecting to see a bear. I didn’t — thankfully, or unfortunately, depending on how brave I was feeling that day.






Tip



If you’re doing this in one day like I did, start at Stanley Park early. It’s very easy to lose track of time here.







One of the things I liked most was how quickly the scenery changed. One minute I was surrounded by trees, and the next I was looking out over the water with downtown in the distance.
Having only recently moved here, it was one of those moments where Vancouver started to feel a little less like a place I’d moved to and a little more like a place I was beginning to know.

title: A Perfect Day in Vancouver
text:
Vancouver Aquarium
From the park, it was a short walk to the Vancouver Aquarium.
The sea otters were doing their absolute best to steal the show, and, frankly, they had no competition. I probably spent twenty minutes just watching them float around.
They appeared to have mastered the art of having absolutely nowhere else to be.
It’s a good reminder of how much marine life is sitting right off the coast here.

title: A Perfect Day in Vancouver
text:
Vancouver Lookout
By the afternoon, I made my way downtown to the Vancouver Lookout for a completely different perspective — literally.
Seeing the whole city laid out from up there, with the mountains in the background and the water on every side, made it click just how much Vancouver is shaped by its geography.
After seeing the city from ground level all morning, it was nice to finally see what all the walking had added up to.
Worth the elevator ride up.

title: A Perfect Day in Vancouver
text:
Gastown
By this point, I had walked enough that my feet had started submitting complaints.
So I ended the day exactly the way you’re supposed to end a good day of exploring: a beer in Gastown.
Cobblestone streets, the steam clock doing its thing, and a cold drink after a full day of walking — a solid way to close out my first real tour of the city.




Four stops, one day, and I think I understand Vancouver a little better now.
I’m still very new to the city, but one thing I’ve already noticed is how easy it is to go from forest to ocean to skyline to historic neighbourhood without really feeling like you’ve left the city at all.
There are still plenty of places I haven’t seen, which is probably a good thing.
My feet may disagree, but I think I’m going to like it here.

title: About
text:
I grew up in Mysore, India, where I developed an appreciation for good food, travel, and probably an unhealthy attachment to Mysore Pak.



I studied Electrical Engineering at PES University in Bangalore.



After graduating, I spent five years at Bosch as a Senior ML Engineer, working on anomaly detection, computer vision, and NLP.
Five years of teaching machines to detect unusual things seemed like a reasonable amount of time to spend thinking about what I wanted to do next.



I decided to continue my studies and moved to Canada to start the Master of Data Science at UBC.
So, after five years of industry experience, I voluntarily went back to school.
This seemed like a good idea at the time.

title: About
text:
Why data science
I was inspired by projects such as Project Euphonia, Project Relate, and Project Lookout.
What I find particularly interesting about these projects is that the technology isn’t the end goal. The goal is to help people communicate, move, and live more independently.
That’s the kind of ML work I want to keep doing.
Accessibility is the thread that runs through most of the problems I want to work on: using technology to make everyday systems more useful and inclusive for more people.

title: About
text:
When I’m not doing ML

🌍 Travel
I love travelling and exploring new places. I’m particularly interested in experiencing a place rather than simply checking its landmarks off a list.
Getting lost somewhere interesting is generally preferable to following a perfectly optimized itinerary.


🍜 Food
I like trying new restaurants and exploring different cuisines.
I consider this research.
The methodology is mostly eating.


🎸 Guitar
I’m currently learning to play guitar.
Progress so far: enough to make the neighbours aware that I am learning guitar.
The long-term objective is to eventually produce something that sounds intentional.


🏖️ Vancouver
I’ve only recently moved to Vancouver, but the combination of mountains, ocean, beaches, and city life has made it a pretty easy place to like.
I’m also still collecting evidence on whether I can survive the weather.
